title: Cochlear Hair Cells
intro: Hair cells turn sound and head motion into electrical signals. They do not fire spikes: deflecting the bundle of stiff stereocilia on top opens mechanically gated channels, the cell depolarises in proportion, and ribbon synapses release transmitter continuously onto auditory nerve fibres, which do spike. In the mammalian cochlea one class of hair cell senses sound and another amplifies it, and the auditory nerve's spike trains are among the best-modelled spike trains in neuroscience.

items: Transduction: stereocilia are linked by fine tip links; deflecting the bundle towards the tallest row stretches them and opens mechanoelectrical transduction channels within microseconds. The gating-spring model describes the channel as opened by tension in an elastic element (Corey & Hudspeth 1983; Howard & Hudspeth 1988).

Inner hair cells (IHCs): about 3,500 per human cochlea in one row. They are the true sensory cells: almost all auditory nerve fibres (type I, about 95 per cent) contact IHCs, each IHC driving 10 to 30 of them.

Outer hair cells (OHCs): about three times as many, in three rows. They change length with membrane voltage thanks to the motor protein prestin (Zheng et al. 2000), feeding energy back into the basilar membrane: the cochlear amplifier, which gives sharp tuning and a large dynamic range and produces otoacoustic emissions.

Ribbon synapses: an IHC releases transmitter at a dense body (the ribbon) that holds a pool of vesicles, allowing sustained, graded release. Release follows the waveform of low-frequency sounds, so auditory nerve fibres phase-lock to tones up to about 4 to 5 kHz in cat (Johnson 1980).

Auditory nerve fibre types: fibres contacting the same IHC differ in spontaneous rate and threshold, from high-spontaneous, low-threshold fibres to low-spontaneous, high-threshold ones (Liberman 1978); together they cover a wider range of loudness than any one fibre.

Tonotopy: position along the cochlea maps to frequency, so each hair cell and fibre has a characteristic frequency. In turtles and frogs, hair cells are also tuned electrically by their own membrane resonance (Crawford & Fettiplace 1981).

Active bundles: hair bundles can oscillate spontaneously; theory places them near a Hopf bifurcation, which explains amplification of faint sounds and compressive nonlinearity (Choe, Magnasco & Hudspeth 1998; Eguiluz et al. 2000). Vestibular hair cells in the inner ear's balance organs use the same machinery.

Meddis (1986): the classic inner hair cell synapse model, with transmitter moving between a factory, a free pool and the cleft. It reproduces adaptation and the spontaneous rate of auditory nerve fibres and is cheap to run; Sumner et al. (2002) revised it with calcium-controlled release.

Auditory periphery models: the Zilany-Bruce-Carney model (Zilany et al. 2014; Bruce, Erfani & Zilany 2018) chains a middle ear filter, nonlinear cochlear filters with OHC control, an IHC stage and a power-law synapse to produce realistic spike trains for any sound. It is the standard for generating auditory nerve input.
Filterbanks: simpler models use gammatone filters or Lyon's cascade of asymmetric resonators (CARFAC; Lyon 2017) followed by half-wave rectification, compression and a spike generator.
Hopf oscillator models of the bundle (Eguiluz et al. 2000) capture amplification with a single nonlinear equation per channel.

blocks.text: What this means for your SNN

items: For audio input, use a cochlear front end: a filterbank, an IHC-like rectifier and adaptation stage, and several spiking fibres per channel with different thresholds. The Spiking Heidelberg Digits dataset (Cramer et al. 2020) was made this way and is a standard SNN audio benchmark.
Phase-locked spike timing carries pitch and location information below a few kHz; above that, only rates and envelopes remain. A rate-only encoder throws much of this away.
Hardware cochleas (silicon cochleas and the Dynamic Audio Sensor) emit address-events like event cameras and can feed neuromorphic chips directly.
